params.question: According to the National Mental Health Survey (NMHS) 2016, what is the approximate lifetime prevalence of mental disorders among Indian adults?

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: This significantly underestimates the burden. The NMHS 2016 — sampling 34,802 adults across 12 states — found a much higher figure, reflecting that mental disorders are far more common than many clinicians assume.
Correct. The NMHS 2016 found that approximately 1 in 7 Indian adults will experience a mental disorder in their lifetime, with a current (past-year) prevalence of 10.6% and a treatment gap of 80–85%.

While the mental health burden is substantial, this overstates the NMHS finding. Common mental disorders (depression, anxiety, somatoform) dominate the distribution, but the overall lifetime prevalence is 13.7%.
This is roughly double the actual figure. The 80–85% treatment gap is high, but the lifetime prevalence itself is 13.7%, not 30%.

overallFeedback.feedback: The correct answer is 13.7%. The NMHS 2016, India's largest nationally representative mental health survey (34,802 adults, 12 states), found a current prevalence of 10.6% and a lifetime prevalence of ~13.7%, with an 80–85% treatment gap.

Correct! The NMHS 2016 documented a lifetime prevalence of ~13.7% — roughly 1 in 7 Indian adults — with common mental disorders contributing the largest share and an 80–85% treatment gap across most categories.

interactions.label: The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 was enacted to provide the delivery framework for

params.question: The Mental Healthcare Act 2017 was enacted to provide the delivery framework for mental health services in India, while the NMHP addresses legal rights and protections.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: This statement is false — it swaps the roles of India's two mental health pillars. The NMHP (1982) provides the delivery framework for mental health services, while the Mental Healthcare Act 2017 provides the legal framework of rights and protections. Keeping this distinction clear is essential for community practice.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct — this statement reverses the two pillars. The NMHP (1982) provides the delivery framework, integrating mental healthcare into primary care across districts via the DMHP. The MHCA 2017 provides the legal framework, establishing patient rights including advance directives and prohibiting inhumane practices such as chaining.

params.question: A 52-year-old woman with poorly controlled diabetes visits your PHC for a routine follow-up. Based on the recognition-and-referral framework, what is the appropriate mental health screening approach for this patient?

answers.text: Screen only if she spontaneously reports mood symptoms

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Opportunistic screening alone misses many cases. Patients with chronic physical illness have a significantly higher prevalence of comorbid mental disorders and warrant proactive, systematic screening at every encounter.

answers.text: Systematically screen her, as comorbid mental disorders are more prevalent in chronic physical illness

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. The recognition-and-referral framework emphasises systematic screening for patients with chronic illness (diabetes, hypertension, epilepsy) because comorbid mental disorders are more prevalent in this group and often go undetected.

answers.text: Refer her directly to the District Mental Health Programme without screening

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Direct referral without initial screening is neither practical nor appropriate. The PHC doctor's role is to first screen using quick tools (e.g. the two-question depression screen) and identify warning signals before deciding on referral.

answers.text: Defer mental health screening until her diabetes is well controlled

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Deferring screening is counterproductive — comorbid mental disorders often worsen glycaemic control and physical disease outcomes. Early identification through systematic screening enables timely intervention.

overallFeedback.feedback: The recognition-and-referral framework recommends systematic — not just opportunistic — screening for patients with chronic physical illness (diabetes, hypertension, epilepsy), as comorbid mental disorders are significantly more prevalent and worsen physical outcomes.

Correct! Patients with chronic physical illness should receive systematic mental health screening at every PHC encounter. The two-question depression screen takes under 60 seconds and can identify warning signals early.
